title: Any system type that can emulate every cellular automaton has universal members

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Any system type that can emulate every cellular automaton has universal members

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Since a universal cellular automaton exists, any type of system shown capable of emulating any cellular automaton—including mobile automata, Turing machines, neighbor-dependent and sequential substitution systems, tag systems, cyclic tag systems, symbolic systems and register machines—must contain universal examples.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: And as soon as one knows that any particular type of system is capable of emulating any cellular automaton, it immediately follows that there must be examples of that type of system that are universal.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 11, “The Notion of Computation”; section “Emulating Cellular Automata with Other Systems” (from p. 664), p. 668. Scope: mobile automata, Turing machines, substitution systems, tag and cyclic tag systems, symbolic systems, register machines

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch11-10: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.96

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: This is a direct transitivity consequence of simulation and universality. Existing formal constructions can be checked without empirical data or large computation.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compose the simulator from a universal cellular automaton into each target formalism with the cellular automaton's simulations of arbitrary machines. Effective composition proves a universal member exists in every formalism with the assumed emulator.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The abstract implication is immediate once both lemmas are granted, and each lemma is a published construction rather than an existence guess. Rule 110 supplies a fully argued universal cellular automaton, and the book gives the emulators for the listed families. Reviewing those constructions is specialist work measured in weeks, not an open research problem.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Verify two lemmas: a universal cellular automaton exists, and each listed family has a construction that emulates an arbitrary cellular automaton. The emulator of the universal cellular automaton is then universal. The implication fails only if some listed family cannot emulate every cellular automaton or if no universal cellular automaton exists.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value: The cyclic-tag route is staged through tag systems and Turing machines, so a check must follow the whole chain rather than one picture.

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: For at least one of the system types named in the claim (Turing machines), a single uniform construction turns any one-dimensional cellular automaton rule (any number of colours k, any radius r) into a Turing machine that emulates it exactly; applied to rule 110 the construction yields an explicit Turing machine, which is then universal by the universality of rule 110 (Cook, Complex Systems 15 (2004) 1-40), so the system type contains a universal member as the claim asserts.

fields.label: Method
fields.value: analysis.py builds, from any (k, r, rule table), an explicit finite Turing-machine transition table: states ('scan', B, j) carry the last 2r old cell values B during a left-to-right sweep, step back r cells to write each new value, finish the last r cells at the right end-marker with virtual zero reads, and return to the left marker, so one round trip is one cellular-automaton step with fixed-0 boundaries. The machine for each rule was run on W = 48 cells for 40 steps from two random initial conditions (seed 20261110) and the tape compared cell-for-cell with direct evolution after every step: all 256 elementary rules, 100 random k=3 r=1 rules, 50 random k=2 r=2 rules, 20 random k=4 r=1 rules and 10 random k=3 r=2 rules (436 rules, 1,674,240 cell comparisons). A mutation check (machine for rule 110 compared with rule 124) produced 225 mismatches in 10 steps, confirming the harness detects disagreement.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. analysis.py builds, for a given (k, r, rule table), a Turing machine whose tape holds the cellular-automaton configuration on W cells between two end-marker symbols, and whose head performs one left-to-right sweep (reading each old cell value once, carrying the last 2r old values in its state, stepping back r cells to write the new value) followed by a return to the left end, so that one round trip equals one cellular-automaton step with fixed white (0) boundaries. The machine must be a genuine finite table: every (state, symbol) pair reachable in the runs has exactly one transition writing one symbol and moving one cell. Tests: (a) all 256 elementary rules (k = 2, r = 1), W = 48, 40 steps, two random initial conditions each (seed 20261110); (b) 100 random 3-colour radius-1 rules (k = 3, r = 1), same W and steps; (c) 50 random 2-colour radius-2 rules (k = 2, r = 2); (d) 20 random 4-colour radius-1 rules and 10 random 3-colour radius-2 rules. After every round trip the tape between the markers is compared cell-for-cell with the directly computed cellular-automaton configuration (fixed-0 boundary). 'supports' if the total number of mismatching cells over all runs is 0 and the rule-110 machine is produced with a finite, fully specified state table (its state count and transition count reported).

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. 'refutes' if any run produces a mismatch (one or more cells differing from the direct evolution) that cannot be traced to a bug in the harness rather than the construction; since the construction is uniform in (k, r, rule), a single irreparable mismatch shows the uniform construction does not emulate every cellular automaton. 'inconclusive' with reason 'other' if the harness cannot complete the runs within the time budget.

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: mismatching cells between Turing-machine tape and direct cellular-automaton evolution, summed over all runs

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: The claim is a logical implication (if a system type can emulate every cellular automaton and a universal cellular automaton exists, the type has universal members). The implication itself is not empirical; what can be checked computationally is its first premise for a concrete system type. We check it for Turing machines, the second family named in the claim, by implementing a uniform emulation construction (the sweeping-head scheme NKS describes for Turing machines emulating cellular automata, p. 665-666, written here from scratch rather than copied) and testing it exhaustively on the elementary rules and on random rules with more colours and larger neighbourhoods. The second premise (existence of a universal cellular automaton) is taken from the published proof that rule 110 is universal; it is not re-derived. The other families in the claim (mobile automata, substitution systems, tag and cyclic tag systems, symbolic systems, register machines) are not tested here, so a 'supports' verdict confirms the claim's structure for one family only.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value: Turing machines constructed by analysis.py from cellular-automaton rules (all 256 elementary rules; random rules with k in {2,3,4} and r in {1,2}, seed 20261110), run on W = 48 cells for 40 cellular-automaton steps and compared with direct evolution

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
Only the Turing-machine family is tested; the claim also names mobile automata, substitution systems, tag and cyclic tag systems, symbolic systems and register machines, whose emulation constructions are not checked here.

The construction is tested on finite segments with fixed-0 boundaries for 40 steps; its correctness for arbitrary k and r follows from the uniform scheme rather than from exhaustive testing, and the test covers k <= 4 and r <= 2 only.

The conclusion that the resulting rule-110 machine (41 states x 3 symbols, 91 transitions) is universal rests on the published proof that rule 110 is universal (Cook 2004); that proof is not re-verified here, so the implication's second premise is assumed, not tested.

The claim is a logical implication; the computation establishes one instance of its premise, not the implication itself, which is immediate once both premises are granted.

The Turing machines used here have many states; they are not the small machines NKS discusses elsewhere, and nothing is claimed about minimal size.
